In American politics, the Southern strategy refers to a strategy by some Republican Party candidates of gaining political support in the Southern United States by appealing to racism against African Americans.[1][2][3]

During the 1950s and 1960s, the African-American Civil Rights Movement achieved significant progress in its push for desegregation in the Southern United States. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, in particular, largely dismantled the system of Jim Crow laws that had enforced legal (or de jure) segregation in the South since the end of Reconstruction Era. During this period, Republican politicians such as Presidential candidate Richard Nixon worked to attract southern white conservative voters (most of whom had traditionally supported the Democratic Party) to the Republican Party,[4] and Senator Barry Goldwater won the five formerly Confederate states of the Deep South (Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi, and South Carolina) in the 1964 presidential election. In the 1968 presidential campaign, Nixon won Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, and Tennessee, all former Confederate states, contributing to the electoral realignment that saw many white, southern voters shift allegiance from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party during this period.

From 1890 to 1908, the white Democratic legislatures in every Southern state enacted new constitutions or amendments with provisions to disenfranchise most blacks[22] and tens of thousands of poor whites. Provisions required payment of poll taxes, and complicated residency, literacy tests, and other requirements, which were subjectively applied against blacks. As blacks lost their vote, the Republican Party lost its ability to effectively compete in the South.[23] There was a dramatic drop in voter turnout as these measures took effect, a decline in African-American participation that was enforced for decades in all southern states.[24]

The "Year of Birmingham" in 1963 highlighted racial issues in Alabama. Through the spring, there were marches and demonstrations to end legal segregation. The Movement's achievements in settlement with the local business class were overshadowed by bombings and murders by the Ku Klux Klan, most notoriously in the deaths of four girls in the bombing of the Sixteenth Street Baptist Church.[35]

After the Democrat George Wallace was elected as Governor of Alabama, he emphasized the connection between states' rights and segregation, both in speeches and by creating crises to provoke Federal intervention. He opposed integration at the University of Alabama, and collaborated with the Ku Klux Klan in 1963 in disrupting court-ordered integration of public schools in Birmingham.[35]

Many of the states' rights Democrats were attracted to the 1964 presidential campaign of conservative Republican Senator Barry Goldwater of Arizona. Goldwater was notably more conservative than previous Republican nominees, such as Dwight D. Eisenhower. Goldwater's principal opponent in the primary election, Governor Nelson Rockefeller of New York, was widely seen as representing the more moderate, pro-Civil Rights Act, Northern wing of the party (see Rockefeller Republican, Goldwater Republican).[36]

In the 1964 presidential campaign, Goldwater ran a conservative campaign that broadly opposed strong action by the federal government. Although he had supported all previous federal civil rights legislation, Goldwater decided to oppose the Civil Rights Act of 1964.[37] He believed that this act was an intrusion of the federal government into the affairs of states and, second, that the Act interfered with the rights of private persons to do business, or not, with whomever they chose, even if the choice is based on racial discrimination.

Goldwater's position appealed to white Southern Democrats, and Goldwater was the first Republican presidential candidate since Reconstruction to win the electoral votes of the Deep South states (Louisiana, Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, and South Carolina). Outside the South, Goldwater's negative vote on the Civil Rights Act proved devastating to his campaign; the only other state he won was his home one of Arizona, contributing to his landslide defeat in 1964. A Lyndon B. Johnson ad called "Confessions of a Republican," which ran in the North, associated Goldwater with the Ku Klux Klan. At the same time, Johnson’s campaign in the Deep South publicized Goldwater’s support for pre-1964 civil rights legislation. In the end, Johnson swept the election.[38]

At the time, Goldwater was at odds in his position with most of the prominent members of the Republican Party, dominated by so-called Eastern Establishment and Midwestern Progressives. A higher percentage of the Republican Party supported the Civil Rights Act of 1964[37] than did the Democratic Party, as they had on all previous Civil Rights legislation. The Southern Democrats mostly opposed their Northern Party mates — and their presidents (Kennedy and Johnson) — on civil rights issues. At the same time, passage of the Civil Rights Act caused many black voters to join the Democratic Party, which moved the party and its nominees in a progressive direction.[39]

Game Dev Tycoon, released in late 2012, is what it sounds like: a Tycoon style simulation game based on video game development. One plays as a small developer who starts out as a garage developer and works to build a major game studio. The game takes place over the course of a few in-game decades, with events and consoles parallel to equivalents stretching from the 90's to today.

Gameplay

In short, Game Dev Tycoon mostly revolves around a cycle of spending one's budget to prepare for future development, starting development on a game, and keeping the development of the game running as smoothly as possible. How well the game ultimately is reviewed and sells will depend on the Design and Tech stats of your employees, the combination of a the Topic and Genre, correctly investing into different aspects of a game, and so on.

Although the moment-to-moment gameplay of Game Dev Tycoon can be a bit plain at points, there are many elements that enrich the experience. Though you start out as a one-person team, you will soon have to manage a full team and consider the talents, weaknesses, and endurance of each team member. Employees can be trained at a fairly low cost, but can't do this while making games. Thus, you have to switch between improving your team and giving them appropriate tasks.

Game Development is a multi-stepped project that demands good decisions across an entire cycle. For example, there are six main genres of games (Action, Adventure, RPG, Simulation, Strategy, and Casual) and dozens of Topics (Fantasy, Horror, Romance, Spy, Wild West, etc). Though all genres are quickly available, one will have to slowly unlock topics, matching them to genres that your team is capable of working with. For example, a Superhero game will be a good match for the Action and RPG genres, but not for Simulation or Adventure genres. And once one decides to make an Action game, they will need a team with a proportionately higher Tech Skill than the RPG genre would require.

Even after a game concept is realized, there are still important factors to decide before work begins. Most important is what platform to release the game on? Game Dev Tycoon's platforms roughly mirror those of real life, progressing from old "Govodore 64" to the "Wuu" by "Ninvento." These different platforms will become more and less popular over time, be more popular among certain age groups, and attract fans of different genres. In general, Action games perform best on consoles and Adventure games on PC, but otherwise there are a lot of case-by-case examples of genres doing well or poorly on any given platform. Throw in how one needs to buy a license to develop for most platforms, and that using newer tech in games takes older or handheld platforms out of the picture, and there's a lot to consider.

Once development is finally underway, it is a simple matter of tasking the correct people to the best matching job over three stages of development. The main dilemma here will come latter in the game, where even the biggest staff will barely be able to cover all the needed bases of a big project. Again, planning an entire project in advance is key.

The game is also livened up by the occasional event. You can show off your game at the annual E3 stand-in, be the center of controversy when creating a game for Mature audiences, avoid Nigerian scam artists, and so on. Some of these events involve choices without an obvious best answer. If your recent game is buggy and needs a patch, do you take a financial hit to fix it or risk alienating fans? Do you crack down on people who pirate your games? Throw in a few trends (topics and genres becoming more popular for limited times) and Publishers (make a game according to their specifications for a smaller cut of the increased sales), and you have a fair amount of depth.

The main problem with Game Dev Tycoon is how opaque the gameplay is. A lot of important concepts and information is either hard to find or simply has to be known through experience. You might not know that a certain genre doesn't work well on a certain platform until the reviews come in, and setting priorities can be difficult until you've had some failures. There are online guides that outline all of this well, but the game itself should be clearer. As is, it's playable but difficult in the same way many rogue-likes are. You will fail a few times before getting the hang of things.

Presentation

Game Dev Tycoon is the first game from a small indie developer, something that shows in the presentation. Though hardly ugly, the game's graphics are simple. Likewise, the music is pleasant, but easily fades into the background. This can actually be beneficial though, since this lets the necessary information pop out.

One thing that can't be excused is the occasional slowdown. During the most heated parts of development, the game might slow down somewhat as it crunches the numbers being thrown around. It's not horrendous, but a game this simple should not have anything like this. Perhaps this is due to my playing it on an older laptop, but other indie games don't show this problem.

One more thing: the game has a sense of awareness. There are some Easter Eggs here, some achievements there, and so on that will get a chuckle out of most knowledgeable players. I wouldn't call it a funny game, but the flavor is nice.

Realism and Lack Thereof

It would be a bit much to expect a realistic simulator from an indie game, but it's important to review what this entails. You will develop a maximum of one game at a time, and even big games will take less than a year to complete. Once people are hired, they will remain with your company for as long as you'd like. Though platforms and Publishers play a role, it feels like you're the only developer in this world. And you always start as a small indie who works their way up, meaning it will be a long time before you try to enter the console market.

For the most part, these concessions make the game play at a better pace, and equate to less sitting around waiting for the next bit of gameplay. But if you want to lead an alternate Sega to a glorious future, you can't do that here.

Conclusion

Game Dev Tycoon is not a great game. One can argue that it's mediocre at best, especially for the price. That said, the concept alone can be intriguing, and the game offers enough depth for those who take the time to invest in it. If you have enjoyed similar Tycoon games in the past, and the concept sounds interesting, you will likely find the game more than worthwhile. Just be prepared to consult a guide as necessary.

Notes
